scope: Peoples in the world catalogue: 6 retained scenes and 9 retained card-art proposals
creator_message:
can we try to understand why the dominion cards always have the best art? interesetingly i prefer the general art designs you made over the card art, especially in this set.

of the general, my ranking is 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 6, 1 from favorite to least favorite.

card art is 5, 6, 7, 9, and a little of 10, but i dont like 10 or the other very much. the dominion ones always look more painted and i kind okf like that the colors aren't overstated. let's see if we can figure it out

explicit_feedback.general: General scene designs preferred over card art, especially in this set. Dominion images repeatedly feel more painted to the creator, who likes their less overstated colour.
explicit_feedback.approval_scope: Comparative preference and art-direction investigation only. No new final selection, deletion, species rejection, commit or game implementation authorized by this feedback.

inspection.basis: Original inspection covered the complete historical batch; 15 records remain after cleanup.

observations.finding: Dominion uses closely related grey, brown, green-grey and iron tones, with small warm accents. Focal faces, hands and plate carry more definition; much surrounding cloth, smoke and stone merges into broad shadow or visibly broken strokes. Reflections are concentrated on metal.

The same Glimmerfolk design succeeds more strongly for the creator in the lamplit workshop. S2 has saturated blue and amber, a specific fitting gesture and a lived-in courtyard. C3 loses that interaction for a tight lantern-in-doorway portrait, with stronger luminous dots and orange/blue skin accents and a smoother-looking face.

Hessa's household scene retains room, weather and quiet character. C9 remains a liked grounded armed figure. C10 spreads golden highlights across fur, wet roots, reeds and ground, giving the spell obstruction and shiny surfaces much of the image's attention.

Both Crest images have visibly coarse strokes but bright peach-gold skin, crisply highlighted ridges and a sunlit stone setting. This separates the presence of brush texture from the creator's preference for a painted result.
The ferry scene's physical interaction becomes a shield-and-wave display in C2; the luminous ward and spray occupy a large portion of the composition.
C7 is bright and dynamic but liked. C8 is comparatively muted yet not liked much. Neither action nor average saturation alone explains the ranking.

prompt_evidence.quote: Invent a clearly different dramatic composition.
prompt_evidence.interpretation: Possible pressure to escalate staging when translating an existing scene into card art; not proof of a causal mechanism.

prompt_evidence.quote: Ordinary-sized soldier, oppressive service not glorious champion.
prompt_evidence.interpretation: Specific restrained character direction counterbalances generic dramatic-card instructions.

prompt_evidence.quote: The supernatural event is the unsettling return of a person, not a bright visual soul.
prompt_evidence.interpretation: Magic is carried by the character's state and another person's gesture, preserving a quiet figure painting.

prompt_evidence.evidence: Golden storm-break sunlight; a warm golden ward and breaking spray; an enormous stone wedge opening a sunlit path; roots and an open/blocked passage as the main event.
prompt_evidence.interpretation: These briefs place strong effects, warm spectacle or a demonstrated action at the center even though literal rules/stat text was excluded.

working_hypotheses_not_creator_rules: Dominion's selected subjects and specific briefs jointly encourage a cohesive palette, restrained highlights, material differences and contained staging; these may explain the painted quality better than faction identity alone.
Several translations into card art lost the specific human-scale interaction or sense of an inhabited place and emphasized an ability or heroic presentation instead.
Visible brush texture alone does not guarantee the desired painted impression; the handling of form, reflection, colour and edges appears important.

Made people are more human-faced than the other subjects, so subject familiarity and design preference remain confounds. This comparison cannot establish the cause of an 'always' pattern across all historical art.
The scenes and cards differ in framing, subject action, light and sometimes reference inputs; rankings alone cannot isolate one causal variable.

proposed_test_not_executed.subject: C3 Glimmerfolk, fixed identity, pose, composition and scene
proposed_test_not_executed.colour_variant: Change only the colour/light brief toward quieter related tones and smaller high-saturation accents, preserving the blue glimmers and current composition.
proposed_test_not_executed.paint_handling_variant: Retain the current colour families and lighting direction, but use broader matte facial planes, selective edges and highlights, quieter secondary surfaces, and materially distinct skin, wool and stone.
proposed_test_not_executed.interpretation: Compare with the existing control before combining changes; generative editing can still introduce incidental differences. Study scene/story changes separately after testing rendering.
proposed_test_not_executed.status: Not executed. The creator next requested the S5/S6 consistent-lighting test, recorded in lighting-prompts-and-manifest.json.

preservation: All existing PNGs, catalogue review controls and final-reference approvals preserved. No commit created.
